cards.title: Weber, Schek and Blott
cards.prompt: These three had a finished design before they had this result. What was the design called, how long before the paper was it written up, and what does that ordering tell you about what the 1998 paper was actually for?
cards.answer: The VA-File, written up about a year earlier as a technical report dated October 1997. The VLDB 1998 analysis came after the design, not before it: they had to prove the scan was unavoidable before making a scan cheaper counted as a contribution at all. The proof is the justification for the artifact, not its origin.
cards.body: Roger Weber and Hans-J. Schek were at the Institute of Information Systems, ETH Zentrum, 8092 Zurich; Stephen Blott was at Bell Laboratories in Murray Hill. Their working problem was picture retrieval - colour features, 45 dimensions per image. Their famous result is the negative one they hit while trying to justify a positive one.

cards.title: The benchmark that beat the trees
cards.prompt: Two named tree indexes were measured against the dumbest possible alternative. Name both trees, name the alternative, and give the two dimensionality crossovers: where the trees stop winning, and where the winner is nothing anyone would call an index.
cards.answer: An R*-tree and an X-tree, against a plain sequential scan of the whole file. The X-tree is fastest below five dimensions; a simple scan is fastest at five to six; above ten the data-partitioning trees are worse than the scan, and at high dimensionality they lose 'by orders of magnitude'.
cards.body: The real data set was a 50,000-image database: five overlapping regions per picture, nine colour dimensions each, 45 in total. Wall-clock time plotted against dimensionality on a log axis. The crossover is not a tuning artefact - the paper's own 20% block-access threshold predicts it, and the measured curves follow the prediction.

cards.title: A Quantitative Analysis and Performance Study for Similarity-Search Methods in High-Dimensional Spaces
cards.prompt: Name the primary source that closes exact high-dimensional search, its venue and pages, and quote the clause in it that decides whether billion-vector exact search is an unsolved engineering problem or a closed one.
cards.answer: Weber, Schek and Blott, Proceedings of the 24th VLDB Conference, New York, 1998, pp. 194-205. Existing methods are 'outperformed on average by a simple sequential scan if the number of dimensions exceeds around 10' - and any partitioning or clustering scheme 'must degenerate to a sequential scan through all their blocks'. Closed, not unsolved.
cards.body: Twelve pages. An average-case analysis, deliberately, where the prior results were worst-case: lower bounds for space-partitioning, data-partitioning and clustering structures, then wall-clock experiments. Its closing postulate is that all approaches 'ultimately become linear at high dimensionality'. Of its own VA-File it says 'we only sketch the method here'.

cards.title: Why your index has a recall knob and no correctness knob
cards.sub: STOC 1998 to the vector database you are choosing
cards.prompt: If no exact index beats a scan above ten dimensions, what did the field start selling instead - and where in that thing's definition is the price printed?
cards.answer: Approximate nearest neighbour. The price is in the definition itself: return any point within a factor of (1+e) of the true nearest. Error becomes a parameter of the problem rather than a defect in the implementation, so HNSW, IVF and product quantization are not competing solutions to one problem - each is a different price on the same trade.
cards.body: The same year the VLDB paper closed the exact road, Piotr Indyk and Rajeev Motwani paved the approximate one at STOC 1998, its key ingredient locality-sensitive hashing. Their own reading of the state of the art: exact methods 'provide little improvement over the brute-force algorithm which compares the query point to each data point'.

cards.title: When Is "Nearest Neighbor" Meaningful?
cards.prompt: A Wisconsin paper supplies the geometry behind the ETH measurement. What happens to the distance from your query to its nearest and to its farthest neighbour as dimensions are added, at how few dimensions does it start, and why does that leave an index nothing to prune?
cards.answer: They converge - the distance to the nearest data point approaches the distance to the farthest one, so 'nearest' stops distinguishing anything. Beyer, Goldstein, Ramakrishnan and Shaft show it on real data for as few as 10-15 dimensions. Pruning needs regions you can rule out by distance; when all distances are alike, there are none.
cards.body: Four authors at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, published the year after the ETH result. It also lands the methodological charge: most high-dimensional index papers 'are not evaluated versus simple linear scan', and re-reading their own reported experiments often shows linear scan winning anyway.
